newsitem.title: USA: Calif. legislator proposes marijuana research center.
newsitem.headline: Calif. legislator proposes marijuana research center.

text.p: A California state legislator Wednesday proposed setting up a state-funded centre to research the medical uses of marijuana.
State Senator John Vasconcellos, a Democrat, also proposed creating a task force to draw up a statewide plan to distribute marijuana to those who need it for medical reasons.
The proposals were contained in a bill that Vasconcellos said he planned to introduce in the state legislature before the end of this month.

The bill is aimed at clarifying and putting into effect a controversial measure passed by California voters last November that allows sick people to legally use marijuana to ease the pain of illnesses such as AIDS, cancer and glaucoma.

"The voters have spoken. Now the work begins to ensure the people of California's policy is translated into the most effective practical terms for the Californians it's intended to benefit," said Vasconcellos, who supported the medical marijuana measure known as Proposition 215.
The Clinton administration opposed Proposition 215 and has threatened to sanction doctors who prescribe marijuana, which remains an illegal drug under federal law.

Vasconcellos accused the Clinton administration of avoiding research that might find that marijuana could be a safe and effective medicine. "If the federal government is unwilling to conduct real research to benefit sick and dying people, then California will," he said.

Vasconcellos's bill would require the University of California to set up a medical marijuana research centre to study the medical safety and efficacy of marijuana and develop medical guidelines for its use, according to a draft of Vasconcellos's bill.

The bill proposes that the research centre conduct controlled clinical trials on the usefulness of marijuana in treating chronic pain, nausea caused by chemotherapy, glaucoma and other conditions. It calls for the centre to receive $6 million in state funding over three years.
The bill would also create a task force to design "a statewide plan to provide for the safe and affordable testing and distribution of marijuana to all patients in medical need of marijuana."

Vasconcellos's bill says doctors may approve the use of medical marijuana by children under 18 only if they have explained the risks and benefits to the child and to a parent or guardian and the parent or guardian has stated in writing that he or she understands the risks and benefits.
